summary: Malaysia is split. In PENINSULAR Malaysia (and the Federal Territory of Labuan) the roof rat is PROHIBITED as a pet: Rattus rattus is explicitly named in the Fifth Schedule ("Controlled Species") of the Wildlife Conservation Act 2010 (Act 716), and section 117 bars any person from keeping, breeding, selling, buying, importing, or exporting a Fifth-Schedule species — with no captive-bred or domestication exemption, and penalties up to RM50,000 / 3 years (raised by the 2022 Amendment, Act A1646). Note the reversed species-trap: the common fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is NOT scheduled and is kept openly, while R. rattus is named by binomial. In EAST Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak), which have their own wildlife laws, R. rattus is NOT on the state schedules, so keeping it is not barred by wildlife law; commercial breeding/selling needs a Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) animal-business licence under the Animal Welfare Act 2015 (Act 772), and importing needs a state veterinary import permit (Sarawak Form A; Sabah DOVSAI permit + MAQIS clearance). Not CITES-listed. Never release — it is a documented agricultural pest.

kit.problem: Malaysia treats the roof rat (Rattus rattus) very differently by region. In Peninsular Malaysia it is a Fifth-Schedule 'Controlled Species' under the Wildlife Conservation Act 2010, so keeping, breeding, selling, importing, or exporting it is prohibited outright. But in Sabah and Sarawak — which have their own wildlife laws and do NOT schedule R. rattus — keeping it is not barred by wildlife law at all. The practical gap is at the East Malaysia border: because R. rattus is also classified as an agricultural pest, an applicant for a state veterinary import permit (Sarawak's Form A, or Sabah's DOVSAI permit + MAQIS clearance) may be refused on an ad-hoc basis even though no statute requires that refusal for a documented, captive-bred, indoor companion specimen.
kit.ask: Ask the Sarawak State Veterinary Authority (DVS Sarawak) and the Sabah Department of Veterinary Services & Animal Industry (DOVSAI) to confirm in writing whether a captive-bred Rattus rattus kept as an indoor companion is eligible for import-permit consideration (Sarawak Form A under the Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999; Sabah DOVSAI import permit), and whether the species' agricultural-pest classification for WILD populations translates into a categorical administrative bar on documented captive-bred specimens. For Peninsular Malaysia, the only honest ask is informational: confirm with PERHILITAN that there is no exemption order permitting private keeping of a Fifth-Schedule R. rattus.
kit.branch_note: Lever = the state AGENCY in East Malaysia (DVS Sarawak / DOVSAI Sabah), which administers the import-permit discretion — NOT the legislature. In Peninsular Malaysia there is no realistic administrative lever: the prohibition is set in the Fifth Schedule by the federal legislature and was reinforced by the 2022 Amendment, so changing it would require a s.133 ministerial exemption order (precedent is pharmaceutical/scientific only) or a schedule amendment. Pushing the legislature there is not a near-term path; the productive work is the East Malaysia permit-eligibility clarification.

targets.why: Administers Sarawak's Form A import permit (Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999, s.9). The right office to confirm whether captive-bred R. rattus is eligible for an import permit or categorically refused due to pest status.

targets.name: Department of Veterinary Services & Animal Industry Sabah (DOVSAI)
targets.why: Issues Sabah import permits (with MAQIS clearance) for live animals. The right office to confirm import eligibility for a documented captive-bred R. rattus.

targets.name: PERHILITAN (Dept of Wildlife & National Parks, Peninsular Malaysia)
targets.why: Administers Act 716 in Peninsular Malaysia. Informational only: confirm that no exemption order permits private keeping of a Fifth-Schedule R. rattus (the prohibition is absolute).

template.en:
To the Department of Veterinary Services [Sarawak / Sabah]:

I am writing as a private hobbyist researching whether a captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus), kept as an indoor companion animal, may be imported into [Sarawak / Sabah]. I understand that R. rattus is not listed in the state's wildlife protection schedules, and that import of a live animal requires a veterinary import permit ([Sarawak: Form A under the Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999] / [Sabah: a DOVSAI import permit with MAQIS clearance]).

My question is narrow: is a documented, captive-bred R. rattus kept as an indoor pet eligible for import-permit consideration, or is the species categorically refused because wild roof rats are classified as an agricultural pest? If eligibility exists, I would be grateful for the documentary requirements (for example, an origin-country veterinary health certificate and any quarantine conditions).

I am asking only to understand the framework and to act lawfully and responsibly. Thank you for your time and guidance.

[Your name]
[Your contact details]

kit.confidence_notes: Grounded in the Gemini DR (2026-06-11), which cites the primary statutes directly: Act 716 (Fifth Schedule + s.117) and the 2022 Amendment Act A1646 via FAOLEX; the Sabah Wildlife Conservation Enactment 1997 and Sarawak Wild Life Protection Ordinance 1998 (which do not schedule R. rattus); the Sarawak Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999 (Form A) via Sarawak LawNet; and Act 772 via DVS. Direct email addresses for DVS Sarawak and DOVSAI were not confirmed in the DR — the official departmental contact pages are given instead; obtain the current import-division email before sending. The East Malaysia permit-denial risk is an inference from the species' pest classification, not a documented refusal, and is exactly what the clarification seeks to resolve.

keep.why: PENINSULAR Malaysia: Rattus rattus is explicitly named in the Fifth Schedule ('Controlled Species') of the Wildlife Conservation Act 2010 (Act 716), and s.117(1) provides that no person shall keep a Fifth-Schedule species. Unlike protected (First Schedule) species there is no private keeping-licence mechanism for controlled species, and there is no captive-bred or domestication exemption; penalties were raised to RM50,000 / 3 years by the 2022 Amendment (Act A1646). EAST Malaysia (Sabah/Sarawak): R. rattus is NOT on the state wildlife schedules (the Sarawak Ordinance expressly does not protect Muridae), so keeping it is not barred by wildlife law there — treat keeping as unregulated/legal in Sabah and Sarawak, subject to Act 772 welfare duties and any local pest by-laws.
keep.governing_law: Peninsular: Wildlife Conservation Act 2010 (Act 716) Fifth Schedule + s.117(1); Act A1646 (2022 amendment). East Malaysia: Sabah Wildlife Conservation Enactment 1997 and Sarawak Wild Life Protection Ordinance 1998 (R. rattus not scheduled).

breed.why: PENINSULAR: breeding requires keeping, which s.117 prohibits for a Fifth-Schedule species; additionally ss.118-119 of Act 716 ban hybridisation of controlled species without the Director General's written permission, and any hybrid is itself deemed a controlled species. There is no commercial captive-breeding licence pathway for controlled species. EAST Malaysia: not barred by wildlife law; commercial-scale breeding is an 'animal business' under the Animal Welfare Act 2015 (Act 772) needing a DVS premises licence (welfare/facility inspection), while non-commercial hobby breeding is exempt from the commercial licence but still bound by Act 772 welfare duties.
breed.governing_law: Peninsular: Act 716 s.117 + ss.118-119 (hybridisation). East Malaysia: Act 772 s.35 (animal-business licence).

sell_give.why: PENINSULAR: s.117(1) of Act 716 prohibits any person from selling or purchasing a Fifth-Schedule species; both commercial sale and private transfer are barred. EAST Malaysia: not barred by wildlife law — commercial retail needs a DVS pet-shop/premises licence under Act 772, and private gratuitous transfer between individuals is unregulated by wildlife law but subject to Act 772 welfare duties (including the no-abandonment / no-release rule).
sell_give.governing_law: Peninsular: Act 716 s.117(1). East Malaysia: Act 772 s.35 (premises licence).

transport.why: PENINSULAR: s.117(1) of Act 716 expressly bars importing and exporting a Fifth-Schedule species (the 2022 Amendment added re-export), and any domestic movement implies possession, which is itself prohibited — so MAQIS/DVS will not permit a R. rattus import destined for Peninsular Malaysia. EAST Malaysia: import is permit-gated, not barred — Sarawak requires a Form A 'Permit to Import' under the Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999 (60-day validity) plus an origin-country veterinary health certificate; Sabah requires a DOVSAI import permit + MAQIS e-permit clearance through a designated port. Not CITES-listed. Never release.
transport.governing_law: Peninsular: Act 716 s.117(1) + Act A1646 (import/export/re-export ban). East Malaysia: Sarawak Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999 s.9(1) (Form A); Sabah DOVSAI import permit + MAQIS.

restrictions.summary: PENINSULAR Malaysia (incl. Labuan): the roof rat is a Fifth-Schedule 'Controlled Species' under the Wildlife Conservation Act 2010, so keeping, breeding, selling, buying, importing, or exporting it is prohibited under s.117 — there is no private-keeping permit and no captive-bred exemption; penalties reach RM50,000 / 3 years (Act A1646, 2022). Do not keep, breed, sell, or move R. rattus in Peninsular Malaysia.
steps: In Peninsular Malaysia, do not keep/breed/sell/import R. rattus — it is a Fifth-Schedule controlled species (no permit pathway)
Never release a roof rat (it is a documented agricultural pest)

restrictions.summary: EAST Malaysia (Sabah/Sarawak): R. rattus is not scheduled, so keeping is not barred by wildlife law. Commercial breeding/selling needs a DVS animal-business / pet-shop licence under Act 772 (facility/welfare inspection). Importing needs a state veterinary import permit: Sarawak Form A (Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999) + an origin-country health certificate; Sabah a DOVSAI permit + MAQIS e-permit. Confirm with the state DVS that a captive-bred specimen is eligible (pest classification may prompt ad-hoc refusal).
steps: Commercial breeding/sale (Sabah/Sarawak): obtain a DVS animal-business / pet-shop licence (Act 772)
Import to Sarawak: apply for Form A + origin-country veterinary health certificate
Import to Sabah: obtain a DOVSAI import permit + MAQIS e-permit clearance

restrictions.fees: DVS animal-business licence set by state DVS

inquiry_focus: (1) PERHILITAN (Peninsular): confirm that Rattus rattus is listed in the Fifth Schedule (Controlled Species) of the Wildlife Conservation Act 2010, so that keeping/breeding/selling/importing it is prohibited under s.117, and that no exemption order permits private keeping. (2) DVS Sarawak / DOVSAI Sabah (East Malaysia): R. rattus is not on the state wildlife schedules — is a documented, captive-bred R. rattus kept as an indoor companion eligible for an import permit (Sarawak Form A / Sabah DOVSAI permit), or is it categorically refused because wild roof rats are an agricultural pest? What documentation (health certificate, quarantine) is required?
